title: The Stations of the Cross
hook: fourteen stops along the way of the cross, prayed in some churches

segments.voice: Yesterday, stripping the altar: a table cleared to the wood while a psalm was read in the dark. Your line was bare. What surface did you leave empty? Day one thousand thirty-one.

Along the side walls of some churches hang small carvings or paintings, spaced out like mile markers. A man standing before a judge. A woman holding out a cloth. A stranger pulled from the crowd to carry a beam of wood. On Good Friday, and in some churches on other Fridays too, people walk from one to the next. They stop, they pray, they move on. In Jerusalem, pilgrims walk a route through the old streets that tradition calls the way of sorrows, stopping at the same scenes. On a church wall, the walk comes to wherever you live. Today, the Stations of the Cross.

The stations are a walk with stops. Tradition counts fourteen in the usual set, starting with Jesus condemned and ending with his body laid in the tomb. Some of the stops come straight from the Gospels. Others come from tradition. Take one from the Gospels first. Luke says that as they led Jesus away, the soldiers grabbed a passerby. In the King James: "they laid hold upon one Simon, a Cyrenian, coming out of the country, and on him they laid the cross, that he might bear it after Jesus." A man on his way into the city, minding his own business, ends up walking directly behind Jesus with the weight on his shoulders. Some readers hear in that phrase, after Jesus, the language of following. Then, a little further on, Luke has women in the crowd weeping, and Jesus turns to them: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children." Even on that road, he turns to face them, and his words point past his own suffering to troubles still ahead for the city and its children. Other stations, like Jesus falling under the cross, or a woman named Veronica wiping his face, come from tradition rather than the Gospel text. The stations are prayed in Catholic and Anglican churches, and in some others. Some versions use only scenes found in the Gospels, and some Protestants prefer it that way. Whichever set is used, the shape is the same. You don't take in the whole story at once. You walk a few steps, you stop at one moment, you stay with it, and then you walk again. It's the story at walking pace.
screen: `SOME FROM THE GOSPELS, SOME FROM TRADITION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk and pause fourteen times. Around the room is enough, or down a hallway, or in place if you need to. Take a few slow steps, and stop. One breath. Then walk again. At each stop, let one face come to mind: someone carrying something heavy right now. Don't count too carefully, and don't hurry. If you pray, you can name each person to God at each stop. If you don't, simply hold them there for one breath, the way Simon held the beam. The bell holds the time.
The Stations of the Cross. A walk with stops, from Jesus condemned to Jesus laid in the tomb, prayed one scene at a time.
screen: `THE STATIONS OF THE CROSS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: step by step with him. Today, when something feels too heavy to face whole, take it one stop at a time, and pause between the stops. Day one thousand thirty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics, Anglicans and some other Christians pray the Stations of the Cross, especially on Good Friday, walking from station to station in church with a short reading and prayer at each.

notes: Claims rule: the number fourteen is attributed to tradition ('tradition counts fourteen in the usual set'); no history or dates of the devotion are given. The practice's fourteen pauses follow the outline.
Veronica and Jesus's falls are named as coming from tradition, not the Gospels; meeting his mother is not mentioned. Confirm wording is respectful to Catholic Keepers.
Which churches pray the stations (Catholics, Anglicans, 'some other churches') and that some versions use only scriptural scenes, preferred by 'some Protestants', should be confirmed.
The Via Dolorosa is described only as 'a route through the old streets that tradition calls the way of sorrows'; confirm.
Editor pass: the 'language of following' reading of Luke 23:26 is now attributed to some readers rather than stated as fact.
Second editor pass: cut the unsourced 'and churches say so plainly'; the line on who prays the stations no longer reads as every Catholic and Anglican.
Audit pass: Luke 23:28 was read as Jesus attending to the women's grief; in context (23:29–31) it is a warning of coming disaster for Jerusalem, and the line now says so.
